content_html:
From Retina to Reconstructed Recall

There is no long-term “photographic” store. The brain reconstructs a memory by reactivating and integrating distributed traces, which are continually shaped by meaning, inference, emotion, and prior experiences.

The early sensory trace (iconic memory) is high-capacity but ultra-brief; longer-term representations are distributed (not photographic). Recall arises from reactivating distributed patterns, shaped by semantics, logic/inference, emotion, and other memories.

Summary

Stage What Happens Key Brain Systems Vulnerabilities / Influences
Retina Phototransduction; initial encoding of luminance and chroma. Rods, cones; retinal ganglion cells → LGN Optical constraints; adaptation
Sensory (Iconic) High-capacity, ultra-brief persistence. Early visual cortex (V1/V2), sensory buffers Rapid decay; masking
Encoding & Consolidation Attention selects; hippocampus binds; systems consolidation over time. Frontoparietal WM; hippocampus; sleep networks Interference; attention limits; stress
Distributed Storage Features stored in modality-specific cortices with semantic and affective links. Temporal/occipital cortex; PFC; amygdala Schema assimilation; emotional salience
Reconstruction / Recall Reactivation of distributed patterns to assemble a plausible memory. Hippocampus–cortex loops; DMN Semantics, logic, emotion, other memories reshape content
